This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 47-3016.00, Helpers--Roofers: helping roofers through duties requiring less skill, including using, supplying or delivering materials and tools and cleaning work areas and equipment. Official scope: Help roofers by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. O*NET lists core tasks including the following (the page lists 18 tasks and displays the first 5 by default): inspecting completed roofs to ensure watertightness; positioning ladders, scaffolds and hoists to deliver materials to roofs; cleaning work areas and equipment; maintaining tools and equipment; and assisting skilled roofers installing and repairing roofs, flashing and roof surfaces. Common job titles include Roofer Helper, Roofer Apprentice and Roofing Apprentice. Coverage note: U.S. wage and employment data presented on O*NET's 47-3016.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, so this page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (47-3016.00). In the U.S., it is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0), with Bright Outlook. This page does not extrapolate U.S. classifications to job titles, qualifications or wages in mainland China.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional roofing assistance task package (for practicing the process only; it does not represent any real enterprise, project or data). Draft a plan explaining: (1) how to use a fictional work order and roof information to assist systematically with roof installation or maintenance, covering location and drawing number, roof type, slope and waterproofing requirements, tile, membrane, flashing and fastener specifications, lifting materials onto the roof, hoisting and positioning, substrate inspection and cleaning, height, edge and opening protection, weather and work windows, and post-work cleaning and inspection; identify missing information needing clarification, including roof structure and waterproofing details, site, support and hoisting conditions, safety, access and work permit requirements, material deliveries and schedule coordination; (2) how to design completion and review points for a fictional materials and work record, covering fields and definitions, location and batch identifiers, materials, specifications and quantities, lifting onto the roof, positioning and fastening, waterproofing, slope and flashing, inspection, abnormalities, rework and outstanding items, and original records and revision trails; (3) how to write a shift and work summary suitable for handover, covering location—materials and specifications—lifting onto the roof and positioning—waterproofing and fastening—inspection, outstanding items and recommendations; (4) how to record and retain materials and work data and distinguish public information from controlled project and supplier information; and (5) how to pause, review, isolate and report height, hoisting, weather or waterproofing risks, matters beyond job authorization or safety risks. Use public sources and simulated data, without real enterprise or project data.

Fit signals | Work activity importance for U.S. O*NET 47-3016.00 shows handling and moving objects (86), performing general physical activities (81), inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (68), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (67), identifying objects, actions, and events (66), and organizing, planning, and prioritizing work (64) as the occupation's most important activities. Work context indicates common outdoor exposure to all weather (74% daily), mostly irregular schedules (77% irregular), prolonged standing (69% continually or almost continually), frequent face-to-face discussions (86% daily), time pressure from schedules and weather windows (57% daily), common contaminant exposure (49% daily), and serious consequences of error (29% extremely serious, 14% very serious, 24% serious). If you are willing to provide hands-on assistance with materials, tools and roofs, can thoroughly perform lifting materials onto roofs, positioning, inspection and cleaning according to skilled workers' instructions and drawings, and take responsibility for work safety, process quality and site order, daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports, for 47-3016.00 work context and tasks, exposure to heights (17% once a week or more, 13% once a month or more), common outdoor exposure to all weather (74% daily), mostly irregular schedules (77% irregular), common hazardous equipment exposure (29% daily), common contaminant exposure (49% daily), serious consequences of error (29% extremely serious, 14% very serious, 24% serious), and time pressure from schedules and weather windows (57% daily). This occupation works with roofs, tiles, membranes, flashing and work at height. Inadequate height, edge or opening protection, improper hoisting, handling or material stacking, waterproofing, slope or flashing errors, or inadequate substrate inspection or fastening may cause falls, material waste, roof leaks, schedule delays and compliance risks. O*NET places it in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0), with Bright Outlook. Its education section reports that 46% indicate a high school diploma or equivalent is required, 30% less than a high school diploma, and 12% a postsecondary certificate (the three categories listed). The page indicates no transferable skills meeting the minimum score threshold. If working outdoors in all weather, at height and on roofs is difficult, or you struggle with a pace varying by weather and schedules and possibly involving overtime and rush work, or are unwilling to take responsibility for safety and process coordination, treat these as practical costs.

Responsibility judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same assignment: deliver sound technical work by completing lifting materials onto roofs, positioning, fastening, waterproofing, inspection and cleaning according to drawings, skilled workers' instructions and procedures, producing usable materials and work records; manage safety, compliance and boundaries by working and keeping records according to height, edge, opening, hoisting, handling, tool, cutting, weather and work permit requirements, distinguishing public information from controlled project and supplier information and handling it under procedures, and avoiding unauthorized scaffold erection or dismantling, hoisting or actions beyond your remit; and accept defined responsibility for your own lifting materials onto roofs, positioning, fastening, inspection, cleaning and records, while referring matters beyond authorization or involving specialized work and major safety issues to appropriate roles or organizations under procedures. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as an assistance plan and explanation of materials and work records for a fictional work order, or a review of height, hoisting or waterproofing abnormality handling, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | This page's Helpers--Roofers is the exact O*NET occupation 47-3016.00. Work falls into several categories: (I) materials and preparation—unloading materials and tools from work vehicles, unrolling membranes as required, hoisting asphalt and roofing materials with ropes and pulleys or carrying materials up ladders to roofs; (II) heights and positioning—positioning ladders, scaffolds and hoists to deliver materials to roofs, and positioning and fastening tiles, membranes and flashing; (III) installation and repair assistance—helping skilled roofers install and repair roofs, flashing and roof surfaces, and covering roofs with roofing felt or asphalt strips before tiles, slate or synthetic materials are laid; (IV) inspection and maintenance—inspecting completed roofs to ensure watertightness, locating worn or damaged areas, performing emergency leak repairs and general maintenance, and maintaining tools and equipment; and (V) cleaning and closeout—cleaning work areas and equipment, sweeping and clearing roofs, and cleaning drains, downspouts and gutters.

Direct answer | Central risks extend beyond whether tiles can be laid to four failure categories with substantial consequences: safety and personal injury failures, including heights, falls and roofs, weather, heat and cold, hoisting, handling and material stacking, and tool, cutting and machinery injuries; quality and rework failures, where inadequate waterproofing, slope, flashing or fastening causes roof leaks and rework; finished-work failures, where improper substrate inspection, cleanup or protection damages roofs; and recordkeeping and traceability failures, where inaccurate materials and inspection data prevent responsibility from being determined.

subject.name: Helpers--Roofers
subject.summary: Helpers--Roofers is the exact O*NET/SOC occupation 47-3016.00: helping roofers through duties requiring less skill, including using, supplying or delivering materials and tools and cleaning work areas and equipment. Core tasks include inspecting completed roofs to ensure watertightness; positioning ladders, scaffolds and hoists to deliver materials to roofs; cleaning work areas and equipment; maintaining tools and equipment; and assisting skilled roofers installing and repairing roofs, flashing and roof surfaces. Common job titles include Roofer Helper, Roofer Apprentice and Roofing Apprentice. Official scope: Help roofers by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. Coverage note: U.S. wage, employment and industry data presented on O*NET's 47-3016.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, so this page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (47-3016.00). It is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0), with Faster than average growth (5% to 6%) for 2024—2034 and Bright Outlook. This page does not constitute safety, specialized work, occupational health or legal advice.
